This meme highlights a humorous and slightly jarring comparison between two titans of middle-grade literature: Nikki Maxwell from Dork Diaries and Greg Heffley from Diary of a Wimpy Kid. The contrast lies in the linguistic "edginess" found in their respective series. On one hand, the post points out that Nikki Maxwell used a specific ableist slur in the very first installment of her seriesâa reflection of the different editorial standards or perhaps a more unfiltered attempt at capturing "mean girl" dialogue in the late 2000s. In contrast, Greg Heffley, despite being frequently characterized by readers as a "sociopath" or a cynical anti-hero, maintains a remarkably sanitized vocabulary. Jeff Kinneyâs Wimpy Kid series is famous for its "G-rated" middle-school angst, where even a word like "crap" is off-limits, replaced instead by milder frustrations.
âThe humor stems from the irony of character perception. Greg Heffley is often analyzed by the internet as a deeply flawed, selfish individual, yet his "journal" remains linguistically pure over eighteen books. Nikki, who is generally framed as the relatable protagonist and "good girl," ends up holding the record for the more controversial vocabulary. This comparison taps into a specific brand of internet nostalgia that re-examines childhood media through a modern lens, finding these small, forgotten detailsâlike a single word choice in a pink-covered diaryâand pitting them against the long-standing purity of a rival series to highlight how much the landscape of children's publishing has shifted.

How to tell if your computer has been hacked.

Most people think their antivirus is a perfect shield, but a manual security audit is the only way to find "digital parasites" that are in your computer.

First, check for "Ghost Users."

Press Win + R and type netplwiz.

If you see an account name you donât recognize, like "Admin1" or a random string of letters, a hacker may have created a backdoor to stay logged in even after you change your password.

Second, hunt for background parasites.

Open Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc and check the "Startup" tab.

Look for "High Impact" apps with gibberish names from "Unknown Publishers."

If you find something like win_driver.exe sitting in your AppData folder, itâs likely a virus.

Third, see who your PC is "talking" to.

Open CMD as Admin and type netstat -ano.

If your browser is closed but you see an "ESTABLISHED" connection to a foreign IP address, your data is currently being sent to an outside server.

You can paste those IPs into VirusTotal to see if theyâre flagged as malicious.

Finally, check for "Invisible" Tasks in your Task Scheduler.

Hackers often hide scripts under boring names like "Chrome Cleanup" that only run at 3 AM.

If a task points to a weird .bat or .vbs file, that's a red flag.

But make sure to always research a file before deleting it so you don't break your OS, this is strictly for educational purposes only.
